nodes.label: Rules of criminal law: purpose of criminal law and burden/standard of proof (prosecution proves beyond reasonable doubt)
Theory of criminal law: purposes of punishment and criminalisation (retribution, deterrence, rehabilitation, protection, denunciation)
Theory of criminal law: the relationship between law and morality (Devlin v Hart debate)
Theory of criminal law: the harm principle as a basis for criminalisation (Mill)
Classification of crimes: conduct crimes and result (consequence) crimes distinguished
Actus reus: requirement of a voluntary act
Actus reus: involuntariness negates actus reus (e.g. Hill v Baxter, reflex/spasm, automatism-type acts)
Actus reus: general rule that omissions do not give rise to liability
Exception to omissions rule: statutory duty to act
Exception to omissions rule: contractual duty to act (Pittwood)
Exception to omissions rule: duty arising from a special relationship (Gibbins v Proctor)
Exception to omissions rule: voluntary assumption of a duty of care (Stone v Dobinson)
Exception to omissions rule: duty arising from a public office (R v Dytham)
Exception to omissions rule: duty arising from creation of a dangerous situation (Miller)
Causation: factual causation - the 'but for' test (R v White, R v Pagett)
Causation: legal causation - defendant's act must be an operating and substantial cause (R v Smith)
Causation: novus actus interveniens breaks the chain of causation
Causation: intervening medical treatment only breaks the chain if independent and so overwhelming it renders original act insignificant (R v Cheshire, R v Jordan)
Causation: victim's own act only breaks the chain if unforeseeable/not within the range of expected responses (R v Roberts, R v Williams)
Causation: the 'thin skull' rule - defendant must take victim as found (R v Blaue)
Mens rea: direct intention - the defendant's aim or purpose
Mens rea: oblique intention - virtual certainty test and jury may find intention (R v Woollin)
Mens rea: subjective recklessness - defendant foresees an unjustified risk and takes it anyway (R v Cunningham, R v G)
Mens rea: negligence - falling below the standard of a reasonable person as a basis of liability
Strict liability offences: liability without proof of mens rea for at least one element
Transferred malice: mens rea transfers where the same type of crime is committed against an unintended victim (R v Latimer)
Transferred malice does not apply across different types of crime (R v Pembliton)
Coincidence of actus reus and mens rea: both must exist at the same point in time
Coincidence rule extended via the continuing act doctrine (Fagan v MPC)
Coincidence rule extended via a single series of acts doctrine (Thabo Meli, Church)
Murder actus reus: unlawful killing of a reasonable person in being and under the King's Peace
Murder mens rea: intention to kill or cause grievous bodily harm (malice aforethought)
Murder as an offence: actus reus and mens rea combine to define the offence of murder
Murder: mandatory life sentence and the role of voluntary manslaughter defences in reducing liability
Loss of control (s54-55 Coroners and Justice Act 2009): partial defence reducing murder to voluntary manslaughter
Loss of control element: defendant's acts/omissions resulted from a loss of self-control (s54(1)(a))
Loss of control: loss of control need not be sudden but a considered desire for revenge is excluded (s54(4))
Loss of control element: qualifying trigger required - fear of serious violence and/or things said or done constituting circumstances of an extremely grave character (s55)
Loss of control qualifying trigger: fear of serious violence from the victim (s55(3))
Loss of control qualifying trigger: things said or done amounting to circumstances of an extremely grave character giving a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged (s55(4))
Loss of control exclusion: sexual infidelity alone cannot qualify as a trigger (s55(6)(c))
Loss of control exclusion: defendant cannot rely on a trigger they incited to provide an excuse for violence (s55(6))
Loss of control element: a person of the defendant's sex/age with normal tolerance and self-restraint might have reacted similarly (s54(1)(c))
Diminished responsibility (s52 Coroners and Justice Act 2009): partial defence reducing murder to voluntary manslaughter
Diminished responsibility element: abnormality of mental functioning arising from a recognised medical condition
Diminished responsibility element: abnormality substantially impaired ability to understand conduct, form rational judgment or exercise self-control
Diminished responsibility element: abnormality provides an explanation for the defendant's conduct in the killing
Unlawful act (constructive) manslaughter: involuntary manslaughter based on death caused during an unlawful act
Unlawful act manslaughter element: defendant committed an unlawful act (a criminal offence)
Unlawful act manslaughter element: the act was dangerous - a sober and reasonable person would recognise risk of some harm (R v Church)
Unlawful act manslaughter element: the unlawful and dangerous act caused death
Gross negligence manslaughter: involuntary manslaughter based on a grossly negligent breach of duty causing death
Gross negligence manslaughter element: existence of a duty of care owed by the defendant to the victim
Gross negligence manslaughter element: breach of that duty of care
Gross negligence manslaughter element: breach caused death
Gross negligence manslaughter element: breach was so bad as to be grossly negligent - jury assesses whether it amounts to a crime (R v Adomako)
Common assault under s39 Criminal Justice Act 1988: causing another to apprehend immediate unlawful force, with intention or subjective recklessness
Battery under s39 Criminal Justice Act 1988: application of unlawful force to another, with intention or subjective recklessness
Assault occasioning actual bodily harm (s47 OAPA 1861): assault or battery causing ABH, mens rea only that of assault/battery (R v Roberts, R v Savage)
ABH defined: injury interfering with health or comfort, more than transient or trifling (R v Miller/R v Chan-Fook)
Malicious wounding/GBH (s20 OAPA 1861): unlawfully and maliciously wounding or inflicting grievous bodily harm
Wounding defined: break in both layers of the skin (JJC v Eisenhower)
Grievous bodily harm defined: really serious harm (DPP v Smith, R v Saunders)
s20 mens rea: intention or subjective recklessness as to some harm being caused, not necessarily as to the level actually caused (R v Mowatt, R v Parmenter)
Wounding/GBH with intent (s18 OAPA 1861): unlawfully and maliciously wounding or causing GBH with intent
s18 mens rea: specific intention to cause really serious harm (or intention to resist arrest) - direct or oblique intention only
Theft under s1 Theft Act 1968: dishonestly appropriating property belonging to another with intention to permanently deprive
Theft element: appropriation - assumption of the rights of an owner (s3), can occur even with owner's consent (R v Gomez, R v Hinks)
Theft element: property includes money and all other property, real or personal, subject to exclusions (s4)
Theft element: belonging to another - property belonging to a person with possession, control or a proprietary interest (s5)
Theft element: property received under an obligation to deal with it in a particular way is treated as belonging to another (s5(3), R v Hall)
Theft element: dishonesty - statutory exclusions under s2 and the Ivey test for dishonesty (Ivey v Genting Casinos)
Theft element: intention to permanently deprive, including treating property as one's own to dispose of regardless of others' rights (s6)
Robbery under s8 Theft Act 1968: theft plus use or threat of force immediately before or at the time of stealing, in order to steal
Robbery element: force or threat of force used on any person immediately before or at the time of the theft
Robbery element: force must be used in order to steal - the purpose nexus between force and theft (R v Robinson, R v Dawson and James)
Burglary under s9(1)(a) Theft Act 1968: entering a building/part as a trespasser with intent to steal, cause GBH, or commit criminal damage
Burglary under s9(1)(b) Theft Act 1968: having entered as a trespasser, stealing or attempting to steal, or inflicting or attempting to inflict GBH
Burglary element: entry - effective and substantial entry into the building (R v Collins, R v Brown)
Burglary element: building or part of a building, including inhabited vehicles/vessels (s9(4))
Burglary element: trespasser - entering without permission or exceeding the permission given (R v Jones and Smith)
